column2: For the sake of all beings' meditation, the formless one took on form; he himself is Shiva in person, who shows loving kindness to his devotees.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, fourth book, the Kotirudra Samhita, chapter 43: the exposition of knowledge. Suta said: Listen, all you sages, to the knowledge of Shiva as I have heard it; I shall tell this great secret, whose nature is supreme liberation.
The individual self, a portion of his own portion, deluded by ignorance and helpless, thinks "I am another"; freed from that, it becomes Shiva.
Pervading all, Shiva in person is the all-pervader in all creatures; lord of the conscious and the unconscious, Shankara himself is everywhere.
The discerning man who takes up the means to see him, resorting to the path of Vedanta, gains the fruit of seeing him.
Just as fire pervades and abides in every piece of wood, and whoever churns that wood surely sees it, without doubt,
so the discerning man who practises devotion and the other means here surely sees that Shiva; there is no doubt of it.
Shiva, Shiva, Shiva alone — there is nothing else at all; through delusion Shankara always appears as of many forms.
As the ocean, or clay, or gold takes on manifoldness through limiting adjuncts, so does Shankara.
The distinction of effect and cause does not really exist; it is only by a deluded understanding, and in its absence it vanishes.
When a sprout from a seed displays manifoldness, in the end there is only the seed again, and the sprout perishes.
The knower is the seed; the sprout is held to be the modifications; when they cease, he is the knower again — there is no need to deliberate on this.
It was determined and declared in an assembly of Narada, the Kumaras, Vyasa and Kapila.
All is Shiva and Shiva is all; there is no difference at all. How then does one see the manifold, and how again the oneness?
Just as the one light called the sun is seen by people as manifold, especially in water and the like, so is he.
Though pervading everywhere, space is not bound by touch; just so the all-pervading god is never bound anywhere.
With ego, he is the individual self; free of it, Shankara himself. The individual self is petty and reaps the fruit of deeds; Shankara is great and untainted.
Just as gold, when mixed with silver and the like, becomes of little value, so is the individual self when joined with ego.
And just as gold, purified by alkali and the like, regains its former value, so does the individual self through purification.
First, having found a true guru and filled with devotion, one performs with the thought of Shiva worship, remembrance and the rest intensely.
By that understanding all the impurity of sin and the rest leaves the body, and then ignorance is destroyed when one becomes a knower.
Then the individual self, free of ego and of pure understanding, attains the state of Shankara again by Shankara's grace.
Just as one's own form is seen in a mirror, so one sees Shambhu everywhere; this is well established.
This knowledge should always be known: the whole world is made of Shiva; Shiva is to be known by the all-knowing wise as all-pervading.
He is liberated while living; when the body falls away, he merges into Shiva. The body is under the sway of past karma, and the knower is held to be distinct from it.
He should not rejoice on gaining good nor be angry on gaining ill; one who is even-minded amid the pairs of opposites is called a knower.
By self-yoga or by discrimination of the principles, one seeking liberation should go out of the body as out of a body;
then he merges into Sadashiva, liberated and free of separation. The root of knowledge is spirituality, and of that, devotion to Shiva;
of devotion, love is said to be the root; of love, hearing; of hearing, the company of the good; and of the company of the good, a wise guru.
When knowledge is thus complete, one is surely liberated. Hence whoever is a knower should always worship Shambhu alone.
Endowed with single-minded devotion, he should worship Shambhu again and again; in the end he attains liberation — there is no need to deliberate on this.
For the attainment of liberation there is no god greater than Shankara, taking refuge in whom one turns back from worldly existence.
Thus, O brahmins, I have told you what was determined from the various words of the sages who gathered; it should be carefully held in the mind.
First it was given by Shambhu to Vishnu before the linga; by Vishnu to Brahma, and by Brahma to Sanaka and the others.
Whatever world is seen, from Brahma down to a blade of grass, all of it is Shiva alone; that god is called Shiva.
Then that knowledge was told to Narada by Sanaka and the others; by Narada to Vyasa, and by him, compassionate, to me.
And by me to you; and by you it should be carefully established for the good of the world, for it leads to the attainment of Shiva.
Thus I have told you what you asked, O lords of sages; it should be carefully guarded. What else do you wish to hear?
Vyasa said: Hearing this, the sages attained supreme bliss; bowing, they praised him again and again with voices choked with joy.
The sages said: Disciple of Vyasa, salutation to you; you are blessed, best of Shaivas. You have let us hear the supreme thing, the unsurpassed knowledge of Shiva.
By your grace the confusion of our minds is gone; we are content, having received from you the true knowledge of Shiva that gives liberation.
Suta said: This should not be told to an unbeliever, to one without faith, to a deceiver, to one not devoted to Mahesha, nor to one unwilling to listen, O brahmins.
Having examined the Itihasas and Puranas, the Vedas and shastras again and again, and extracted their essence, Vyasa told it to me.
By hearing this even once, sin is reduced to ashes; the undevoted gains devotion, and the devotee's devotion grows.
On hearing it again, true devotion arises, and on hearing it once more, liberation; therefore those who seek the fruit of enjoyment and liberation should hear it again and again.
When his will arises, then this is brought about. He alone knows all, and no one knows him.
Five recitations should be made with the supreme fruit in view; one then obtains it, without doubt — this is the word of Vyasa.
Nothing is hard to obtain for one who has heard this excellent teaching; by reciting it five times, the vision of Shiva is gained.
Ancient kings, brahmins and excellent vaishyas, having heard this five times with understanding, attained the supreme accomplishment.
Whoever even now, intent on devotion, hears this knowledge named after Shiva will obtain enjoyment and liberation.
Vyasa said: Hearing these words, they attained supreme bliss and respectfully worshipped Suta with many kinds of gifts.
With salutations and hymns, preceded by the recitation of blessings, they honoured him with benedictions, content, their doubts cut away.
Content with one another, Suta and those wise sages, regarding Shambhu as the supreme god, bowed to him and worshipped him.
This true knowledge of Shiva is great and very dear to Shiva; divine, it gives enjoyment and liberation and increases devotion to Shiva.
This holy and supreme Samhita, named Kotirudra, the fourth of the Shiva Purana, has been told by me, bringing joy.
Whoever hears it with devotion, or with a collected mind has it heard, enjoys all pleasures here and in the end attains the supreme goal.
Having created it himself and entered it, he remains afar; he has not really entered it, being untainted, of the nature of consciousness.
Just as light is reflected in water and the like without truly entering it, so is Shiva himself.
In truth he himself is all, and the auspicious sequence merely appears; ignorance is only a difference in understanding — there is no other, no second.
In all the schools of philosophy a difference of views is shown, but the Vedantins always proclaim non-duality.
Hearing his guru's words, Sagara gave up his own vow; he destroyed their dharma and changed the style of their hair.
He sent the Shakas away with half their heads shaved, and the Yavanas and Kambojas with their whole heads shaved.
The Paradas were made to wear loose hair and the Pahlavas beards; that great-souled king deprived them of Vedic study and the vashat call.
The whole earth was conquered righteously by that king, and all those kshatriyas, dear one, had long before been made devoid of dharma.
That king, victorious by dharma, having conquered this earth, had a horse consecrated for the horse sacrifice.
As he let it roam, that horse went to the south-eastern ocean, followed by his sixty thousand sons, O sage.
The sage Vasishtha, for a reason, did not stop the father from banishing his own son from the kingdom then.
Near the shore the horse was carried off by Shakra, king of the gods, pursuing his own interest, and taken into the earth.
The great king Sagara, to search for that horse, then had his sons dig up that region on every side.
Then, as the great ocean was being dug, they came upon that primal person, the god Kapila, whose form is the universe.
By the fire that rose from his eyes as he awoke, the sixty thousand were burned; four were left.
Harshaketu, Suketu, Dharmaratha and the heroic Panchajana were the kings who continued his line.
The Lord Hari himself gave him five boons: lineage, intelligence, fame, the ocean as a son, and wealth.
By that deed of his the ocean obtained the name Sagara, and he recovered the sacrificial horse from the ocean.
That greatly famous king performed a hundred horse sacrifices, and there worshipped the gods, glories of Shambhu, O you of good vows.
The marriage mantras reach completion at the seventh step; but Satyavrata did not understand that secret.
In this his great-souled father was displeased, thinking, "The atonement for the family, O brahmin, must be made."
The blessed Vasishtha did not restrain him when his father cast him out, nor did the sage say, "I will consecrate his son."
The strong one bore that observance for twelve years; when the great-souled Vasishtha had no meat,
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 5, chapter 39: the account of the kings born in the line of Vaivasvata. Shaunaka said: How were the sons of Sagara born, heroic and mighty, sixty thousand valiant ones? By what means? Tell us.
Ambarisha was the son of Nabhaga, and from him came Sindhudvipa; Ayutajit was the valiant heir of Sindhudvipa.
The son of Ayutajit was Rituparna of great fame; that king knew the secret of divine dice and was Nala's friend.
Rituparna's son was Anuparna of great splendour; his son was Kalmashapada, also named Mitrasaha.
Kalmashapada's son was famed as Sarvakarman; the renowned Anaranya was the son of Sarvasharman.
Anaranya's son was the learned king Mundidruha; his son was Nishadha, and Rati, also called Khatvanga,
who, coming here from heaven with but a moment of life left, secured the three worlds by his understanding and truth, O sinless one.
His son was Dirghabahu, and his son Raghu; Aja was his son, and from him came Dasharatha.
From Dasharatha was born Rama, righteous and greatly famous, a portion of Vishnu and a great Shaiva, by whom Ravana, descendant of Pulastya, was slain.
His deeds are described in many ways in the Puranas and are famous in the Ramayana; therefore they are not told here at length.
Rama's son was born, famed as Kusha; from Kusha was born Atithi, and his son was Nishadha.
Suta said: Sagara had two wives whose sins were burned away by austerity; Aurva, best of sages, being pleased, gave the two a boon.
Nishadha's son was Nala, and Nala's son Nabhas; from Nabhas came Pundarika, and after him Kshemadhanvan is remembered.
Kshemadhanvan's son was the valorous Devanika; Devanika's son was the lord named Ahinagu.
Ahinagu's heir was the valiant Sahasvat; his son was Virasena, born of the Ikshvaku family.
Virasena's heir was Pariyatra; then came his son named Bala, and from him was born Sthala.
From him came a son born of a portion of the sun, the valorous Yaksha; his son was Aguna, and from him came Vidhriti.
His son Hiranyanabha became a teacher of yoga; he was a disciple of the sage Jaimini, skilled in the knowledge of the self.
From that excellent king, Yajnavalkya of Kosala learned the yoga called Adhyatma, which cuts the knot of the heart.
His son was named Pushya, and his son was called Dhruva; his son was Agnivarna, and his son was named Shighra.
His son named Maru became perfected in yoga; that lord dwells even today in the village called Kalapa.
At the end of the Kali age, with the sages who live there, he will revive the lost solar dynasty in particular.
One chose sixty thousand sons of great strength; the other, graced with the boon, chose one son to continue the line, as she wished.
His son was Prithushruta, and his son is remembered as Sandhi; his son was Amarshana, and his son Marutvat.
His son was Vishvasahva, and his son Prasenajit; his son was Takshaka, and his son Brihadbala.
These past kings of the Ikshvaku line have been proclaimed; now hear of the future kings of that line, most learned in dharma.
Brihadbala's son will be Brihadrana; Brihadrana's son will be Urukriya.
His son will be Vatsavriddha, and his son Prativyoman; his son will be Bhanu, then Divaka, a commander of armies.
His son will be Sahadeva, a great hero; his son Brihadashva, and his son the mighty Bhanumat.
Bhanumat's son will be the valiant Pratikashva, and his son will be Supratika, best of kings.
His son will be Marudeva, then Sunakshatra; his son Pushkara, and his son Antariksha, O brahmins.
His son will be the heroic Sutapas, and his son Mitrachitta; his son Brihadbhaja, and his son named Barhi.
His son will be Kritanjaya, and his son Rananjaya; then Sanjaya, and Maya; and his son Shakya.
Going there and obtaining those many heroic sons, she gave birth to a gourd, which was then divided into separate seeds.
His son will be Shuddhoda, and his son Langala; his son Prasenajit, and his son named Shudraka.
His son will be Runaka, and his son is remembered as Suratha; his son will be Sumitra, at the very end of the line.
This line of the Ikshvakus will end with Sumitra — a line of kings of varied valour, most righteous and of good deeds.
Reaching King Sumitra in the Kali age, that auspicious line will come to an end, and it will flourish again in the Krita age of Brahma.
Thus the kings of the Vaivasvata line, generous in sacrificial fees, sprung from the line of Ikshvaku, have been proclaimed in the main.
Holy and supreme is this creation of Aditya Vivasvat, the god Shraddhadeva, who gives nourishment to creatures.
The man who reads or hears of this creation of Aditya obtains offspring and, having enjoyed supreme happiness here, attains union.
They all grew up in turn in pots filled with ghee, tended by their nurses, boys who increased joy.
Of those great-souled ones burned there by Kapila's fire, a single son named Panchajana became king.
Then Panchajana had a valiant son named Amshumat; his son was Dilipa, whose son was Bhagiratha,
the lord who brought down the Ganga, best of rivers, and led her to the ocean, and made her his daughter.
Bhagiratha's son was the king known as Shrutasena; his son was Nabhaga, a son supremely righteous.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 5, chapter 40: the description of the power of the ancestors. Vyasa said: Having heard of the unsurpassed line of the sun, Shraddhadeva, Shaunaka, best of sages, respectfully asked Suta:
Yudhishthira said: How do men who desire prosperity obtain prosperity? I wish to hear this: doing what does one not come to grief?
Suta said: Hearing the question put by Yudhishthira, Bhishma, knower of dharma, lovingly spoke while all listened.
Bhishma said: Men who lovingly perform shraddha rites, Yudhishthira, obtain all that through the shraddhas, by the grace of the ancestors.
Men desiring fruits always perform shraddhas, intending them for the father and the father's father,
and the father's grandfather, in the three pinda offerings, constantly. The ancestors grant dharma to him who desires dharma, offspring to him who desires offspring,
and prosperity to him who desires prosperity, Yudhishthira.
Yudhishthira said: The ancestors of some are in heaven, those of others in hell; and it is said that the fruit of deeds is fixed for living beings.
How then do the shraddhas offered reach the ancestors? And how can those who are in hell receive that fruit?
I have heard that even the gods in heaven worship the ancestors. I wish to hear this; tell me in detail.
Bhishma said: I shall tell you here, subduer of foes, as I heard it, what my father sang to me long ago when he had gone to the other world.
Shaunaka said: Suta, Suta, long may you live, disciple of Vyasa; salutation to you. You have let us hear a supreme, divine and supremely purifying story.
At the time of my father's shraddha I had raised the pinda; my father, breaking through the ground, asked for it from my hand.
Deciding that this was not a rule seen in the ritual texts, I placed the pinda on the kusha grass without hesitation.
Then my father, pleased with me, said in sweet words, O best of the Bharatas, sinless one:

Through you, who know dharma and are wise, I have a worthy heir; I am delivered, for I made this test, best of men.
shivpurana:9:40.24	Whatever standard a king sets by his righteous conduct, the people follow; they always follow the standard set.
shivpurana:9:40.25	Hear, best of the Bharatas, the eternal dharmas of the Veda: the standard of Vedic dharma has been upheld by you, son.
shivpurana:9:40.26	Therefore, well pleased with you, I lovingly give you an unsurpassed boon, rare in the three worlds; accept it.
shivpurana:9:40.27	Death shall have no power over you as long as you wish to live; only on receiving leave from you shall death have power.
shivpurana:9:40.28	Or what else do you ask? I will give you an excellent boon; tell me, best of the Bharatas, what is in your mind.
When he had said this, I saluted him with folded hands and said: "I have gained my purpose, since you are pleased, giver of honour. I would ask you a question; please answer it yourself."
You have spoken of the sun, Shraddhadeva, increaser of the good line; a doubt has arisen in me about that, which I state before you.
He said to me, "Say it; if you wish, I will tell you." When he had said this, I asked, and the king answered.
Shantanu said: "Listen, dear one, I will answer your question truly; I heard the whole ritual of the ancestors from Markandeya.
What you ask me, dear one, I asked the great sage Markandeya, and he, knowing dharma, told me.
Markandeya said: 'Listen, king: once, as I was looking at the sky, I saw a great celestial chariot approaching between the mountains.
In that chariot I saw a couch, with the radiance of glowing coals, blazing with great splendour, uniform and lovely,
and on it I saw lying a person of blazing splendour, the size of a thumb, like fire placed in fire.
Bowing to him and saluting the lord with my head, I asked him, "How may we know you, O mighty one?"
The righteous one said to me, "You do not have the austerity by which you could recognize me, O sage; I am a son of Brahma.
Know me as Sanatkumara. What may I do for you? The other sons of Brahma are younger than I:
seven invincible brothers, whose lines are established. But we follow the dharma of ascetics, restraining the self in the self.
How does Aditya Vivasvat come to be Shraddhadeva? I wish to hear it with love; cut away this doubt of mine.
As I was born, so I remain; I am known as Kumara, the youth. Therefore my name has been told as Sanatkumara, O sage.
Since you performed austerity with devotion, longing to see me, here I am, seen by you. Blessings on you; what desire of yours may I fulfil?"
When he had said this, I said to him: "Listen, lord: tell me truly the original creation of the ancestors."
Addressed thus, he said to me: "Listen to it all as it is; I will tell you truly, dear one, the auspicious creation of the ancestors.
Sanatkumara said: Long ago Brahma created the gods and told them, 'Worship me.' But, abandoning him, they worshipped their own selves, seeking fruits.
They were cursed by Brahma: 'Deluded, you shall lose your understanding.' Thereupon, knowing nothing, bereft of understanding, they all bowed to the Grandsire
and said to him, 'Show us your favour.' Addressed thus, he told them this, by way of atonement:
'Ask your own sons; then you will regain knowledge.' Told thus, those bereft of understanding earnestly asked their sons.
For the sake of atonement, the gods regained their understanding, and were told by their sons, 'Go, little sons,' O sinless one.
The cursed gods, having been told by their sons, 'Go, little sons,' asked the Creator about it, wishing to understand the word 'son'.
Tell me too the greatness of the shraddha and its fruit, lord, by which the ancestors, pleased, join one to welfare.
Then the god Brahma said to the doubting gods: 'Listen, all you immortals: you are not knowers of Brahman.
Therefore what your sons, those best of knowers, have said to you should be accepted, abandoning doubt; it is so and not otherwise.
Gods and ancestors, dwellers in heaven, worship one another with great love, as givers of the fruit of all desires.'
Sanatkumara said: Then, their doubts cut away and full of love for one another, O tiger among sages, they became givers of happiness by Brahma's word.
Then the gods said to them: 'Since we were called little sons by you, you shall be the ancestors, without doubt.
Surely people will perform rites in the shraddha for the ancestors; nourished by the shraddhas, Soma will nourish the worlds,
the ocean, the mountains and forests filled with moving and unmoving beings. The men who, desiring prosperity, perform shraddhas —
to them the ancestors, ever pleased, will grant prosperity. And those who offer three pindas in the shraddha, with name and lineage —
their fathers and great-grandfathers, wherever they may be, satisfied by the gift of shraddha, will constantly foster them.
Let this word be true, O dwellers in heaven: we shall all be sons and fathers to one another.'
I wish to hear the excellent creation of the ancestors; tell it in particular, great-minded one; show us your favour.
Thus those gods and ancestors, by dharma, became sons to one another; they are renowned on the face of the earth as ancestors of one another.
Suta said: I will lovingly tell you all about the creation of the ancestors, Shaunaka, as Markandeya told it to Bhishma, who asked him,
and as Sanatkumara sang it to the wise Markandeya; I shall tell it to you — it grants the fruit of all desires.
Asked by Yudhishthira, Bhishma, best of the upholders of dharma, lying on his bed of arrows, spoke; hear it, I tell it to you.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 5, chapter 41: the account of the destiny of the seven hunters. Sanatkumara said: Seven are the hosts of ancestors remembered in heaven, best of ascetics: four are embodied and three are without form.
Listen, Bhishma: long ago the sons of Bharadvaja, brahmins, having attained the dharma of yoga, fell from it through misconduct.
Vagdushta, Krodhana, Himsra, Pishuna, Kavi, Khasrima and Pitrivartin — so named, and so in their deeds.
They were sons of Kaushika, dear one, and disciples of Garga; when their father died, they all went to live abroad.
At their guru's direction they were driving a milch cow, a tawny one with a calf of like colour; then they all strayed into wrongdoing.
As they went along, tormented by hunger, out of youthfulness and delusion, O Bharata, a cruel thought arose in them to kill that cow.
Kavi and Khasrima begged them not to, but the two were unable to restrain their brothers then.
The one among them named Pitrivartin, a brahmin who performed the shraddha daily, devoted to the ancestors, said to them all in anger:

If it must be done, let it be done for the sake of the ancestors; let all of us, with collected minds, perform a shraddha.
shivpurana:9:41.18	In this way this cow will attain dharma, without doubt; having worshipped the ancestors righteously, there will be no adharma for us.
Told thus, they all sprinkled the cow, dedicated it to the ancestors and consumed it, O Bharata.
The primal hosts of gods worship them, and so do brahmins and others; first they nourish Soma by the power of yoga.
Having consumed the cow, they all told their guru, "The cow was killed by a tiger; please take the calf."
In his honesty the brahmin accepted the calf; through their false dealing the sin of cow-killing fell upon them.
Then after some time those seven brothers, dear one, met the law of time as their lives ran out.
Through their cruelty, violence and ignoble conduct toward their guru, the seven brothers were born as those who delight in fierce killing:
the strong and spirited sons of a hunter; they were born as seven hunters in Dasharna, discerning in dharma.
Then, devoted to their own dharma, free of delusion, they became deer, shaken with dread, on the lovely mountain Kalanjara.
Reflecting on that very matter, arising from their memory of former births, they lived as forest-dwellers, patient, beyond the pairs of opposites, owning nothing.
All those forest-dwellers were of auspicious deeds and true dharma, free of unrighteous conduct, gifted with the memory of past births.
The dharma they had heard in their former births in the guru's household remained fixed in their minds, turned toward withdrawal even amid worldly life.
Fasting ascetics, they gave up their lives on the mountain; and the places where they fell, O Bharata,
Therefore shraddhas should be given, especially to yogis; for all, a vessel of silver or one containing silver.
are seen even today on Mount Kalanjara, O king. By that deed they were born free of good and bad.
From a good birth they attained a better one, becoming chakravaka birds; the seven lived as water-dwellers in the auspicious land of Sharadvipa.
Giving up the life of mating, those sages, upholders of dharma — Nihsanga, Nirmama, Shanta, Nirdvandva, Nishparigraha,
Nivritti and Nirvrita — are remembered as birds by these names. All those birds were celibate and walked in dharma.
Remembering their births, fully grown, the seven celibates dwelt together, of true dharma, ever free of change.
For what they had done falsely toward their guru out of delusion in their brahmin birth, they took birth among animals, but through the shraddha they gained knowledge.
Since the shraddha had been performed by them, steadfast, for the sake of the ancestors, they obtained knowledge and birth in succession, ever better in quality.
The Brahman they had heard in former births in the guru's household remained as knowledge; therefore one should practise knowledge.
Sumanas, Suvak, Shuddha, the fifth Chhidradarshaka, Svatantra and Suyajna — they are remembered by name as Kulingas.
Of those birds as they roamed there walking in dharma, a certain good event took place there; hear it, great sage.
The shraddha given with svadha placed first pleases the ancestors; having nourished Agni, Soma and Yama,
The king, lord of the Nipas, endowed with power and splendour, surrounded by his women, entered the forest there.
The chakravaka Svatantra coveted the state of that king, seeing him pass by, full of happiness and the splendour of kingship.

If there is any merit, austerity or observance of mine — I am worn out by fasting and unwavering austerity —
shivpurana:9:41.43	by the full fruit of all of it, may I become such a one, a vessel of every good fortune.
Markandeya said: Then two chakravakas, his companions, said, "We two will be your ministers, wishing your welfare and good."
Saying "So be it," his course as a yogi ended then; and thus the two chakravakas also answered with their own words.

Since, speaking of deeds after attaining that dharma of yoga, you ask for such a boon, therefore hear my words:
shivpurana:9:41.47	You will be a king, dear one, in Kampilya, best of cities, and these two will be your ministers, overcome by transgression.
Three did not speak of kingship to the four companions; he again showed favour, and among them Sumanas said:

The curse will have an end; you will regain yoga. This Svatantra will know the cries of all creatures.

Markandeya said: For the welfare of the worlds, dear one, excellent son of Shantanu, I have told you this story; what more do you wish to hear?
The ancestors grant prosperity and abundant offspring, heaven, increase of health, and whatever else is desired.
Even above the rites for the gods, O sage, the rites for the ancestors are distinguished. You are devoted to the ancestors, brahmin sage; therefore you are free of age and death.
The goal of one devoted to the ancestors, O sage, is not reached even by yoga; therefore devotion to the ancestors should be practised especially, great sage.
Markandeya said: Having said this, the lord of gods quickly gave me an eye with true knowledge, hard to obtain even for the gods, and went his yogic way.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 5, chapter 42: the description of the power of the ancestors. Bhishma said: Markandeya, great sage, best of those devoted to the ancestors, what happened after that? Tell me kindly, best of sages.
Chhidradarshin and Sunetra, masters of the Vedas and Vedangas, were born as heirs of learned brahmins, having lived together in their former birth.
Panchala was a Rigvedin and acted as teacher; Pundarika knew two Vedas, a Chandoga and an Adhvaryu.
Then the king, seeing his sinless son Brahmadatta, consecrated him in his own kingdom and attained the supreme goal.
Panchala and Pundarika, having established their sons in their houses, entered the forest and there reached the supreme goal.
Brahmadatta's wife was named Sannati, O Bharata; single-hearted, she delighted with her husband alone.
The remaining chakravakas, the companions, were born in Kampilya as heirs of learned brahmins in a poor family, O king:
Dhritiman, Sumahatma, Tattvadarshin and Nirutsuka — four seers of faults, accomplished in the study of the Veda.
Devoted to yoga and perfected, they all set out, taking leave of one another and bowing to the lotus feet of Shambhu.
All those brahmins said to their father once more: "We will make an arrangement for you by which you will make your living.
Go to King Brahmadatta, the sinless, with his ministers, and recite to him this verse of great meaning.
Markandeya said: Those seven, devoted to the dharma of yoga, moving about Manasa, living on air and water, constantly dried up their bodies.
Pleased at heart, he will give you villages and abundant enjoyments." Having said this much and honoured their guru, they all attained the dharma of yoga and reached supreme peace.
The father of those four great-souled brahmins, having learned the verse from his sons, felt as if his purpose had been fulfilled.
He recited the verse to the king and his two ministers: "Seven hunters in Dasharna, deer on Mount Kalanjara,
chakravakas in Sharadvipa, swans on the lake Manasa — they were born in Kurukshetra as brahmins, masters of the Veda.
They have set out on the long road; why do you linger?" Hearing that, King Brahmadatta fell into a swoon,
and so did his ministers Panchala and Pundarika, O Bharata. Then, remembering that lake and regaining that yoga,
they furnished the brahmin with ample wealth and enjoyments. Consecrating Vishvaksena, subduer of foes, in his kingdom,
Brahmadatta went with his wife to the forest; attaining yoga by his own strength, he reached the goal most hard to attain.
The righteous Pundarika too, attaining the unsurpassed Sankhya-yoga, reached the goal of yoga, perfected and purified by that deed.
Panchalya, having set out the krama recitation and produced the complete Shiksha, attained the station of a teacher of yoga and foremost fame, great ascetic that he was.
That king, surrounded by his women, sported there a long time like Maghavan in Nandana, and returned with his wife to his city.
May the supreme abode of Shambhu, which heroes who long for no rebirth attain, destroy sin today.
When sin of body, mind or speech has been committed, great sage, one should recite this properly, with devotion and endowed with faith.
One is freed from all sins by the chanting of Shiva's name; when this is uttered, of that god of gods,
sin dissolves like an unbaked pot in water. Therefore, when sin has accumulated, one should immediately
repeat this for the quelling of sin, great sage — faithful men should do so abundantly, to attain the fruit of all desires.
Whoever reads or hears this chapter for the sake of prosperity is freed from all sins and attains liberation, without doubt.
He had a supremely righteous son named Anuha; Vibhraja, establishing that son in the kingdom, went to the forest.
He began austerities where those companions were; there the great ascetic lived without food, subsisting on air.
Since that forest was illumined by him, it became well known as Vaibhraja, bestowing perfection in yoga.
There the four birds who followed the dharma of yoga, and the three who had fallen from yoga, gave up their bodies.
In the city of Kampilya those seven great souls were born, with Brahmadatta at their head, all freed from sin.
Four of them retained memory, but three were bewildered. Svatantra was born of Anuha as Brahmadatta of great vigour.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 5, chapter 43: the manner of worshipping Vyasa. Shaunaka said: Tell me now, Suta, whose guru is Vyasa, about the worship of the teacher, and also what should be done at the end of hearing the book.
Suta said: Having heard the supreme story, one should devoutly worship the teacher according to rule; at the end of the book, with a gladdened mind, one should duly give gifts to the teacher.
Then, bowing to the narrator and worshipping him according to rule, the wise man should honour him with ornaments for hands and ears, and with fine garments of silk and the like.
At the conclusion of Shiva's worship he should give a cow with its calf, and make a seat weighing a pala of gold, with a cloth.
Placing on it the auspicious book written in beautiful letters, the wise man should give it to the teacher; he will be freed from the bonds of worldly existence.
A village, an elephant, a horse and other things according to one's means — all these, O sage, should be given to the great-souled reciter.
A Purana properly heard with its prescribed rites is held to be fruitful; this I have said truly, O sage Shaunaka.
Therefore, O sage, one should hear with devotion and with the prescribed rites the Purana, rich in the meaning of the Vedas, giver of merit, the heart of the Shruti.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 5, chapter 44: the account of the birth of Vyasa. The sages said: Tell us of the birth of Vyasa, great-minded Suta, treasury of compassion; by your supreme grace, master, make us fulfilled, lord.
Wishing to take the lovely fisher-girl, the sage touched her right hand with his right hand.
The Vedas have not known your greatness, lord of Uma; you alone are the creator, sustainer and destroyer of the world.
You are the first of all gods, being-consciousness-bliss, the Lord; you have no name or lineage; you are all-knowing, Sadashiva.
You alone are the supreme Brahman, who removes the noose of maya; you are untouched by the three qualities, as a lotus leaf by water.
